sections.title: A packet vanishes
sections.narration: Ever sent a group-project message and then asked, 'Did you get it?' Networks need an answer too. A packet just disappeared. Let's work out how the sender can recover without making the receiver use the same data twice.
bullets: How can it know what arrived?
sections.takeaway: Reliability requires feedback and carefully tracked state.

sections.title: Read the timeline
sections.narration: Here's how to read our picture: sender on the left, receiver on the right, and time moving downward. Sloping arrows show travel time. The arrows coming back are acknowledgments, or ACKs: small messages confirming progress.
sections.takeaway: A timeline separates transmission, arrival, and acknowledgment events.

sections.title: Send one, then wait
sections.narration: Start with one packet. Send it, keep a copy, and wait for an ACK before moving on. That's stop-and-wait. The backup copy might seem extra cautious now, but we'll be very glad we kept it.
sections.takeaway: Stop-and-wait permits one unacknowledged packet at a time.

sections.title: Choose an ACK convention
sections.narration: Our ACK number means 'This is the packet I want next.' So ACK one confirms packet zero. ACK four confirms zero through three. Remember that rule: the number points forward, not to the last packet received.
bullets: ACK n means next expected n
sections.takeaway: Every ACK number here identifies the next packet expected.

sections.title: Notice the idle gap
sections.narration: The sender has finished putting the packet onto the link, but the journey isn't over. The data still has to arrive, and its ACK has to come back. That's quite a lot of waiting for one little packet.
sections.takeaway: Long feedback delay can leave a fast link mostly idle.

sections.title: Separate two kinds of time
sections.narration: Two clocks are involved. Transmission time is how long we take to put the bits onto the link. Propagation time is how long the signal travels. Posting a letter and delivering it are different parts of the job.
sections.takeaway: Transmission time and propagation delay measure different things.

sections.title: Calculate stop-and-wait use
sections.narration: Sending takes one millisecond; the propagation round trip takes twenty. Ignoring other overhead, that's one useful sending millisecond in a twenty-one-millisecond cycle. About four point eight percent. Our sender is spending most of its time waiting around.
sections.takeaway: With negligible ACK cost, utilization is 1 divided by 21, about 4.8 percent.

sections.title: Lose the data packet
sections.narration: Oops, the packet disappears. No ACK comes back. The sender can't tell whether the data was lost, the ACK was lost, or things are just slow. We need a way to avoid waiting forever.
bullets: No new ACK can confirm it
sections.takeaway: A missing acknowledgment leaves the sender uncertain.

sections.title: Expire a timer
sections.narration: Enter the timer. If confirmation doesn't arrive in time, we try recovery. But a timer isn't a detective: it knows we've waited long enough, not exactly what went wrong. A late packet can still show up.
sections.takeaway: A timeout detects missing confirmation, not certain packet loss.

sections.title: Retransmit the saved copy
sections.narration: Send our saved packet again, with the same sequence number. This time it arrives, and ACK one returns. Now the sender can let go of that saved copy and move on. The backup finally earns its place.
sections.takeaway: Retransmission retries the same logical packet.

sections.title: Lose the acknowledgment instead
sections.narration: Let's make the problem sneakier. The data arrives, but the ACK gets lost. The sender retries because it never heard back. Now the receiver has to say, 'Hang on, I've already seen this one.'
sections.takeaway: The sender may retry data that the receiver already has.

sections.title: Recognize the duplicate
sections.narration: The receiver wants packet one, so another packet zero is a duplicate. Don't give its data to the application twice. Just send ACK one again. Two arrivals, one delivery: we don't need two copies of the assignment.
sections.takeaway: Sequence state distinguishes a duplicate from new data.

sections.title: Why alternating bits can work
sections.narration: For basic stop-and-wait, sequence bits can alternate: zero, one, zero, one. With the right starting state and rules about old duplicates, that can work. We're using larger numbers elsewhere to keep the story easy to follow.
sections.takeaway: A small sequence space requires careful assumptions about delayed duplicates.

sections.title: Choose a sensible timeout
sections.narration: Set the timer too short, and we'll keep retrying perfectly good packets. Too long, and recovery feels painfully slow. This delayed ACK shows why choosing the timeout matters. Real protocols can adjust as network delays change.
sections.takeaway: A timer trades quick recovery against unnecessary retransmission.

sections.title: Allow four packets in flight
sections.narration: What if we allow four packets to be waiting for ACKs? That's our sending window. It's a limit on unconfirmed data, not four new cables. We still keep copies in case we need them again.
sections.takeaway: A sender window permits several packets before confirmation.

sections.title: Fill the pipeline
sections.narration: Send zero, one, two, and three without waiting after each one. Now later data travels while earlier ACKs return. Same link, better use of time. Our sender finally has something to do during that long journey.
sections.takeaway: Pipelining overlaps useful transmission with feedback travel.

sections.title: Use cumulative acknowledgments
sections.narration: ACK three says, 'Zero, one, and two are safely received in order. Send me three next.' One ACK can confirm several packets. But if there's a missing packet, we can't claim the whole sequence beyond it.
bullets: An earlier missing ACK may be covered
sections.takeaway: Cumulative ACKs confirm a contiguous prefix of received data.

sections.title: Slide the sending window
sections.narration: Let's start a separate example with ACK two. Packets zero and one are confirmed, so the window slides two places. New packets can enter on the right. The window moves; its size stays the same.
sections.takeaway: Acknowledgments advance the window and permit new transmissions.

sections.title: Go-Back-N: lose packet 1
sections.narration: Send zero through three, and lose packet one. Zero arrives, so the receiver wants one next. We'll pause new sends here. That leaves packets one, two, and three still waiting for confirmation from the sender's point of view.
sections.takeaway: A gap prevents contiguous in-order acceptance in this Go-Back-N model.

sections.title: Discard later arrivals
sections.narration: In this basic Go-Back-N example, the receiver discards two and three because one is missing. It keeps returning ACK one. They're arriving at the door, but they aren't being accepted into the correct sequence yet.
sections.takeaway: A basic Go-Back-N receiver discards out-of-order packets.

sections.title: Retransmit from the gap
sections.narration: The timer runs out for packet one, the oldest unconfirmed packet. Go back and send one, two, and three again. Zero stays confirmed. That's the idea behind the name Go-Back-N: retry from the missing part onward.
sections.takeaway: Go-Back-N retransmits outstanding packets starting at the oldest unconfirmed one.

sections.title: Accept the repaired sequence
sections.narration: Now one, two, and three arrive in order. The receiver sends ACK four, and the sender can release those saved copies. Quick check: four is the next packet wanted, not the last packet that just arrived.
sections.takeaway: Once the gap is repaired, in-order acceptance and window movement resume.

sections.title: Compare the mechanisms carefully
sections.narration: A bigger window can keep the link busier. Compare one, four, and twenty-one packets. It doesn't make the link itself faster. Modern TCP uses related ideas, but tracks bytes and adds more details than this classroom model.
sections.takeaway: Modern TCP is related to ARQ ideas but is not this exact frame protocol.

sections.title: Reconstruct reliability yourself
sections.narration: Here's our toolkit: ACKs confirm progress, timers start retries, sequence numbers spot duplicates, and windows keep data moving. None can fix a permanently broken connection. But when communication can succeed, they help us recover instead of guessing.
sections.takeaway: Recovery needs feedback and state; permanent link failure can still stop delivery.
